title: Agent Kim Reactivated, Explained: How Korea Went from Son Preference to “Daughter Fool” Dads
description: In SBS's Agent Kim Reactivated, a legendary ex-operative gets on his knees before a chaebol chairman — not to dodge a bullet, but to beg leniency for his daughter. Korea has a word for fathers like him: ttalbabo, “daughter fool.” Here's what that word means, how other cultures say it, and the strange statistical reversal underneath it — a country that once had one of the world's most skewed sex ratios at birth now gets cited as a leading example of daughter preference.
drama: Agent Kim Reactivated (김부장, 2026, SBS · Netflix in select regions)
era: Contemporary Korea — the one-generation reversal of son preference, c. 1990–2026

show: Along with the Gods: The Two Worlds
title: Why Does Along with the Gods Have Seven Afterlife Trials? Korea's Ten Kings and 49-Day Judgment Tradition, Explained
description: In Along with the Gods: The Two Worlds (2017), a dead man must pass seven courts of judgment in forty-nine days. Here's the real Korean and Buddhist tradition behind that structure — the Ten Kings of Hell (시왕), the 49-day mourning ritual, and the bodhisattva Ksitigarbha — and how it compares with ancient Egypt, Catholic purgatory, and Japanese Buddhism.
drama: Along with the Gods: The Two Worlds (신과 함께 - 죄와 벌, 2017, film)
era: Traditional Korean Buddhist and folk belief (Joseon Dynasty and beyond)

title: Secret Royal Inspector & Joy, Explained: What a Joseon Inspector Actually Did After Shouting 'Chuldu!'
description: An amhaengeosa (암행어사) was a temporary inspector, appointed in secret by the king from among trusted officials below senior third rank and sent to the provinces in disguise to investigate local magistrates. He carried a sealed letter, itemized instructions, a bronze mapae tablet and a brass yucheok ruler, and filed a mandatory report to the king on his return. Secret Royal Inspector & Joy is built on this real office — and Korea's most famous secret inspector, Bak Mun-su, never officially held the title.
drama: Secret Royal Inspector & Joy (어사와 조이, tvN, 2021)
era: Joseon Dynasty (1392–1910)

title: Agent Kim Reactivated, Explained: South Korea Sent Thousands of Men North — Then Denied They Existed
description: In SBS's Agent Kim Reactivated, a mild savings-bank manager takes off his glasses and becomes the operative the state erased. Code Name 66 is invented. The erasure is not. Here is the real history of South Korea's north-bound agents, the 1968 Blue House raid, the axe murders at Panmunjom, and the survivor who is still waiting for a pension in 2026.
drama: Agent Kim Reactivated (김부장, 2026, SBS · Netflix in select regions)
era: Cold War Korea — north-bound operatives, the 1968 Blue House raid, the 1976 Panmunjom axe incident

title: Goryeo-Khitan War, Explained: What the Records Actually Say About Arab Traders in Goryeo — and What They Don't
description: The KBS drama Goryeo-Khitan War (2023–2024) reaches its climax at Gwiju in 1019. Five years later, the Goryeo court recorded the arrival of a hundred men from Dashi — the Arab world. The entry is three lines long. This article does something the popular version of this story usually skips: it puts the actual text of all three Dashi entries in the History of Goryeo next to the claims built on top of them. The famous cargo of myrrh belongs to a different year than the famous hundred men. No entry names the port. And 'Hermit Kingdom' was never the title of the 1882 book everyone cites — it was Corea: The Hermit Nation, published by a man who had never been to Korea.
drama: Goryeo-Khitan War (고려거란전쟁, KBS2, 2023–2024, 32 episodes) — a war drama covering the third Khitan invasion and the Battle of Gwiju in 1019
era: Goryeo — reign of Hyeonjong (1009–1031) and Jeongjong (1034–1046); the three Dashi entries are dated 1024, 1025 and 1040

show: The Tiger: An Old Hunter's Tale
title: The Tiger, Explained: Joseon Korea Codified a Military Corps for Hunting Tigers
description: In The Tiger (대호, 2015), a hunter faces a tiger alone on a mountain. Centuries earlier the Korean state had answered the same animal very differently — with the chakho gapsa, a military speciality written into the law codes with quotas, entrance examinations and a reward scale. And when it came to actually catching tigers, the state was happy for you to use a trap.
drama: The Tiger: An Old Hunter's Tale (대호, 2015, dir. Park Hoon-jung) — set in 1925, four centuries after the corps described here
era: Joseon Korea — the chakho gapsa, 15th–16th centuries

title: Did Korea Have Slaves? Chuno & the Truth About Joseon's 500-Year Nobi System, Explained
description: In Chuno, slave-hunter Dae-gil sprints across the Joseon countryside to catch a man who has committed no crime except running away. Here's the real history behind Korea's nobi system — how it worked across five centuries, how it compared with American slavery, Russian serfdom, and medieval European bondage, and why the chase was so relentless that it created an entire professional hunting class.
era: Joseon Dynasty Korea (1392–1894)

title: MBC's The King's Doctor, Explained: Why a Grand Queen Dowager's Mourning Dress Triggered Two Political Battles 15 Years Apart in Joseon Korea
description: MBC's The King's Doctor ends with the physician Baek Gwang-hyeon serving King Hyeonjong. In that very reign, a real dispute erupted over exactly how long the Grand Queen Dowager should wear mourning for the late King Hyojong — a Confucian ritual question that put the king's own legitimacy on trial and twice reshaped the Joseon court over fifteen years.
drama: The King's Doctor (마의, also known as Horse Doctor, 2012 MBC)
era: Joseon Dynasty — King Hyojong's death (1659) through the Yesong mourning-rite disputes (1659–1674)

title: Crash Landing on You, Explained: Are North and South Korea Still Technically at War?
description: In tvN's Crash Landing on You, a gust of wind carries a South Korean heiress across the most fortified border on Earth. The romance is fantasy — but the border is real, and so is the reason it exists: the Korean War never formally ended. Here's the armistice that stopped the shooting in 1953, the 'demilitarized' zone bristling with weapons, the flagpole war, the ghost village, and the families still divided seventy years on.
drama: Crash Landing on You (사랑의 불시착, tvN, 16 episodes, 2019–2020 · Netflix worldwide)
era: Divided Korea — armistice regime, 1953–present

title: Crash Landing on You: The Women, Rations and Markets Behind North Korea's Jangmadang
description: In Crash Landing on You, North Korean villagers haggle over goods at a busy market — and most of the traders are women. Here's what the rationing system actually was, why the jangmadang is older than the famine, how it was legalised and taxed, and why women ended up running it.
drama: Crash Landing on You (사랑의 불시착, tvN, 2019–2020)
era: Contemporary North Korea

title: Was Dae Jang Geum Real? Jewel in the Palace and Joseon's Female Physicians, Explained
description: In Jewel in the Palace (대장금, MBC, 2003–2004), a kitchen maid named Jang-geum rises to become King Jungjong's physician. Here's the real history — Joseon's royal kitchen (suraegan), the food-as-medicine idea (sik-chi), and the euinyeo female-physician system that began in 1406 — and how it compares with China, Japan, and medieval Europe's Trota of Salerno.
era: Joseon Korea (15th–16th century)

title: Dae Jo-yeong, Explained: How Goguryeo Refugees Founded Balhae, Thirty Years After Their Kingdom Was Erased
description: KBS's 134-episode Dae Jo-yeong is a hero epic where the hero almost never wins. Goguryeo fell in 668, its ruling class was deported, and Balhae was founded in 698 — on the old territory, not somewhere new. Here is what the records actually say about Cheonmullyeong, the letters Balhae sent to Japan, the fleet that attacked Tang China, and why the 'Balhae was a Tang province' claim cannot explain any of it.
era: Fall of Goguryeo (668) to the founding of Balhae (698) — and Balhae's 228 years, 698–926

title: Why Did King Sejong's Own Scholars Try to Block Hangul? Tree with Deep Roots & the Politics of Korean Literacy, Explained
description: In Tree with Deep Roots, King Sejong is secretly completing a revolutionary new alphabet while a killer stalks Gyeongbokgung Palace. Here's the real history: why a 15th-century monarch designed an entirely new script from scratch, why his own Jiphyeonjeon scholars petitioned against it, and how a single alphabet became the most politically charged document in Korean history — from Joseon's writing monopoly to Atatürk's Turkey.
drama: Tree with Deep Roots (뿌리깊은 나무, 2011, SBS)
era: Early Joseon (15th century)

title: Did Silla Fall in 927? What Taejo Wang Geon Leaves Out
description: Taejo Wang Geon stages 927 at Poseokjeong as the day Silla fell. The Samguk sagi says King Gyeongae died in 927, but Silla ended in 935, when King Gyeongsun submitted to Goryeo.
era: Late Silla & Later Three Kingdoms (889–936)

title: Doctor X: Where Did the Professor's Grip on Korean Hospitals Come From?
description: In SBS's Doctor X, a surgeon's contract refuses rounds, research errands and staff dinners. Korean university hospitals' professor-centered structure traces back to colonial-era Japanese medical education and post-liberation American residency; we found no source for where the rituals themselves came from.
drama: Doctor X: Mafia in White (닥터X: 하얀 마피아의 시대, SBS 2026)
era: 20th-century Korea — colonial period to post-liberation (1926 onward)

show: Guardian: The Lonely and Great God
title: Guardian, Explained: What a Korean Dokkaebi Really Is — and Why 'Goblin' Doesn't Quite Fit
description: The K-drama Guardian (도깨비) streams on some platforms as Goblin — but a dokkaebi is a much stranger, broader figure than that word suggests. Here's what Korean folklore actually says about dokkaebi, why so many of them were drawn with horns, and how Korea, Japan, China and Europe each imagined the things that move in the dark.
drama: Guardian: The Lonely and Great God (도깨비, tvN, 2016–2017)
era: Korean folklore (Goryeo setting & modern day)

title: The East Palace, Explained: Why the Joseon Crown Prince's Home Was the Most Sacred — and Most Cursed — Place in the Palace
description: Netflix's The East Palace opens with a crown prince dead in a palace pond and a king who cannot report it. Joseon's real crown prince quarters were named for the rising sun — and the records that survive are full of buried curse objects, fire, and political ruin. Here is what maehyung was, why kings hushed it up, and how a hall called Jeoseungjeon came to sound exactly like the Korean word for the afterlife.
era: Joseon Dynasty (1392–1910) — the crown prince's quarters, court curse cases, royal legitimacy

title: Netflix's The East Palace: Why a Confucian Kingdom Kept an Official Shaman Inside the City Walls
description: In Netflix's The East Palace, royal sons keep dying and the king quietly sends an exorcist into the crown prince's quarters. The kingdom is invented — but that summons wasn't. Joseon really did run a bureau called the Seongsucheong, staffed by a national shaman, and Confucian officials spent centuries filing memorials against it without getting it closed.
era: Joseon Dynasty (1392–1910) — court shamanism and royal ritual

title: D.P., Explained: Why Military Service Shapes Nearly Every Korean Man’s Life
description: In Netflix's D.P., two conscripts in plain clothes hunt soldiers who ran from their own army. The unit is real — D.P. is commonly glossed as 'Deserter Pursuit' — and so is the institution underneath it: a conscription system that has re-arranged the youth of Korean men since 1949. Here's how Korean military service actually works, what the law calls 'desertion,' why the soldier D.P. teams were abolished in 2022, and why the show's most uncomfortable question is aimed at the organization, not the runaway.
drama: D.P. (디피, Netflix, Season 1 2021 · Season 2 2023, 6 episodes each)
era: Contemporary Korea — conscription and barracks culture, c. 2014–present

title: Empress Ki and Goryeoyang: Goryeo Fashion at the Yuan Court
description: Fourteenth-century sources record a 'Goryeo style' — goryeoyang — in dress, shoes and food at the Mongol court in Dadu, and connect its spread to the many Goryeo women serving in the palace. This article sets out what each source actually supports, and where Empress Ki does and does not appear in it.
drama: Empress Ki (기황후, MBC, 2013–2014, 51 episodes). Streaming varies by region — Netflix in some territories, Kocowa and OnDemandKorea in the United States at the time of writing; check the official platform where you are. The drama's plot — Seung-nyang, Ta-hwan, Tanashiri and the consort selection itself — is fiction and is not fact-checked here.
era: Late Goryeo under Yuan dominance — the Zhizheng reign era of Toghon Temür (1341–1370) at the Mongol capital Dadu, present-day Beijing

title: Is Empress Ki Buried in Korea? The Mystery of the Yeoncheon Tomb Site
description: In Empress Ki (기황후, 2013), a Goryeo tribute woman rises to become empress of a Mongol empire. There's a site in Yeoncheon, Korea, long said to be her tomb — though no burial mound has actually been confirmed there. Did Empress Ki really come home to be buried? Here's what the histories actually say — and why 'said to be her tomb' is very different from 'is her tomb.'
era: Goryeo Dynasty (918–1392)

title: Was Empress Ki Real? Goryeo's Gongnyeo Tribute Women and the Yuan Dynasty, Explained
description: In Empress Ki (기황후, MBC, 2013–2014), a Goryeo woman taken as tribute rises to become Empress of the Yuan dynasty. Here's the real history behind her story — from Goryeo's tribute-women (gongnyeo) system and the Marriage Bureau (Gyeolhon Dogam) to the political rise and fall of Empress Ki herself — and how it compares with the Ottoman devshirme, Chinese 'peace princesses,' and European dynastic marriage.
era: Goryeo Korea / Yuan Dynasty (13th–14th century)

title: Exhuma, Explained: The Iron Stake and the Records We Could Open
description: The records this piece opened are premodern Korean texts; they do not contain Exhuma's stake or its sorcerer, and they are not the kind of material in which a twentieth-century figure would appear. We describe the film from a Korean script, not the film itself. A 1995 government campaign removed metal stakes and we opened its announcement directly, but the purpose attributed to them is unsettled. Of four Jeju passages we opened two in the original, and in those two 地脈, earth veins, does not occur.
era: Goryeo and Joseon Korea through the Japanese colonial period (1910–1945)

title: Why Does Woo Young-woo Trust Gimbap? The Changing History of Korea's Roll
description: Why does Woo Young-woo trust gimbap (kimbap) in Extraordinary Attorney Woo (ENA, 2022)? Every filling shows when it is cut. Yet the roll was never fixed: Korean newspapers and cookbooks from 1925 to 1976 record changing laver advice and new fillings such as danmuji and ham.
drama: Extraordinary Attorney Woo (이상한 변호사 우영우, ENA, 2022)
era: Joseon to present (late Joseon almanacs; 1920s–1990s newspapers and cookbooks; 2020s exports)

title: Faith (The Great Doctor): The Real Princess Noguk
description: In Faith, the king's men save Princess Noguk. In the records, the Yuan-born queen sat at the door to guard King Gongmin in the 1363 Heungwangsa revolt, then died in childbirth in 1365.
era: Goryeo Dynasty (918–1392) — reign of King Gongmin (1351–1374)

title: From Han to Sinmyeong: Why Korean Culture Feels Both Sad and Alive
description: Korean culture feels both sad and alive because of a four-word cycle: han (a knot of unresolved grief), hwabyeong (its suppressed form), hanpuri (releasing it) and sinmyeong (the ecstatic surge of life that can follow). It is one interpretive lens on Korean art, not a measured fact or a fixed national essence. A companion to our Hotel del Luna piece, and one way to read the emotional intensity of the Korean Wave.
era: Korean emotional culture — from folk ritual to the Korean Wave

title: The Turtle Ship Nobody Has Seen: Korea's Most Famous Warship Left No Blueprint — The History Behind Hansan: Rising Dragon
description: Hansan: Rising Dragon spends half its running time in a workshop rather than a battle, because the turtle ship in it is not finished. That is closer to the record than it looks. This article follows the geobukseon from a river in 1413 to a shipyard in 1592 — and past it, to the 1606 memorial that says one turtle ship was kept at each naval command, and the 1795 compilation that preserves detailed drawings and measurements. Turtle ships did not vanish with Yi Sun-sin. What was never preserved is the thing the drawings themselves admit they altered: the exact dimensions of the ships he fought in.
drama: Hansan: Rising Dragon (한산: 용의 출현, 2022, dir. Kim Han-min) — the second film in Kim's Yi Sun-sin trilogy, covering the Battle of Hansan Island in 1592. An extended cut, Hansan: Redux, opened on 16 November 2022 with roughly 21 minutes of additional footage; the version streaming on Netflix from 2 December 2022 is the Redux, not the theatrical cut.
era: Early and mid Joseon — the name 'turtle ship' first appears in the Veritable Records in 1413; Yi Sun-sin's turtle ships are built and first fought in 1592

title: Jang Ok-jung, Explained: Why Could a King Flip an Entire Government Overnight?
description: Hwanguk (환국) was Joseon's sudden, king-driven change of ruling faction: a single royal decision replaced the ruling faction overnight, promoting one faction while dismissing, exiling, or executing many of the other. King Sukjong did it at least three times — in 1680, 1689, and 1694; the Gisa Hwanguk (1689) deposed Queen Inhyeon and raised Lady Jang, and the Gapsul Hwanguk (1694) reversed it. It is the real history behind Jang Ok-jung, Living in Love (2013 SBS).
drama: Jang Ok-jung, Living in Love (장옥정, 사랑에 살다, SBS, 2013)
era: Joseon (late 17th century)

title: The Emperor's Poisoned Coffee: Gojong and the 1898 Assassination Attempt
description: In 1898, opium was placed in coffee served to Emperor Gojong and Crown Prince Sunjong. The official record identifies the coffee pot, the three men involved, and the political struggle that followed.
era: Korean Empire (1897–1910) — the reign of Gojong

title: Arthdal Chronicles, Explained: Korea's Oldest Transmitted Law — and the Stain That Outlived the Sentence
description: Arthdal Chronicles imagines the birth of a state, and keeps returning to one question: who owns whom. The oldest law transmitted for Korea answers it in three provisions described in the surviving passage — including one that lets a thief pay their way out of bondage, and then records that the shame remained afterwards.
drama: Arthdal Chronicles (아스달 연대기, tvN, 2019) · The Sword of Aramun (아라문의 검, 2023)
era: Gojoseon (고조선) — law recorded in the Han shu

title: Shin Don, Explained: Why King Gongmin Gave Power to the Monk Who Took On Goryeo's Nobles
description: MBC's historical epic Shin Don dramatizes one of Goryeo's strangest political gambles: King Gongmin's anti-Yuan purge, and his decision to hand sweeping power to a low-born Buddhist monk with no ties to the aristocracy — a reformer who fell as fast as he rose.
era: Late Goryeo (14th century)

title: Moon Lovers Explained: How King Gwangjong Used Slave Records to Break Goryeo's Powerful Nobles
description: The real King Gwangjong did more than purge rivals. His 956 Slave Review Act and 958 civil service exam weakened Goryeo's powerful regional magnates and remade the monarchy — and the famous statistic about his purges turns out to be two unrelated records fused together.
drama: Moon Lovers: Scarlet Heart Ryeo (달의 연인 - 보보경심 려, SBS, 2016)
era: Goryeo Dynasty — King Gwangjong's reign, 949–975

title: How Did Goryeo Survive the Liao Empire Three Times? Seo Hui, Kang Gam-chan, and the Battle of Gwiju, Explained
description: In the 2023–2024 KBS drama Goryeo-Khitan War, General Kang Gam-chan breaches a dam and sweeps a Liao army off a Korean river. Here's the real history — how a small kingdom outmaneuvered the dominant power of 11th-century East Asia, why Goryeo's victory reshaped the regional order, and how the Battle of Gwiju compares with Tours-Poitiers, Byzantium's long frontier defense, and China's very different response to the same empire.
era: Goryeo Dynasty, 993–1019

title: Goryeo-Khitan War, Explained: How Song and Goryeo Both Made Peace with the Liao
description: In Goryeo-Khitan War (고려거란전쟁), the thrill is General Gang Gam-chan crushing the Khitan army at Guiju. But to grasp what that victory meant, look at the other giant facing the same Liao empire: Song China. Song paid for peace with silver and silk; Goryeo won it on the battlefield. Here's the real history of two very different survival strategies.
era: Goryeo Dynasty (918–1392)

title: The King and the Clown, Explained: Why a Court Clown Could Mock a Tyrant and Live
description: In The King and the Clown (2005), two street performers are pulled into the palace to mock King Yeonsangun to his face. Here's the real history behind it — narye and sandaehui, the court's masked-performance traditions, and the jaein and changu who were classified among Joseon's lowest caste yet briefly licensed to satirize the throne.
drama: The King and the Clown (왕의 남자, 2005)
era: Joseon dynasty (1392–1897)

title: What Happened to a Joseon Gungnyeo After She Left the Palace?
description: Netflix's The East Palace gives us Saeng-gang, a palace maid who hears the dead. The kingdom is invented, but her job was real — a ranked, salaried career entered in childhood and held, in principle, for life. Court custom reserved death inside the walls for a very narrow circle around the king, so an ageing gungnyeo had to go. Here is what the Korean record says about how that career ended, and what a few senior sanggung built in place of a pension.
era: Joseon Dynasty (1392–1910) — palace women, court service and the end of service

title: Taejo Wang Geon, Explained: Why Did King Gungye Claim He Could Read Your Mind?
description: Gungye's mind-reading in KBS's Taejo Wang Geon comes from the Goryeosa, which quotes him claiming the \"Maitreya mind-reading method\"; here is who it targeted and what Wang Geon kept of his state.
era: Later Three Kingdoms (late 9th – early 10th century)

title: Sungkyunkwan Scandal, Explained: Why Joseon Korea's 'Fair' Exam Wasn't as Fair as It Looked
description: In Sungkyunkwan Scandal, a poor young woman disguises herself as a man just to sit Korea's national exam. But the drama's real fantasy isn't the disguise — it's the idea that the exam was ever a level playing field. Here's the real gwageo system, what a new Cambridge study of 14,258 exam passers actually found, and how Korea's answer compares to China, Japan and the West.
era: Joseon Dynasty — set during the reign of King Jeongjo (r. 1776–1800)

title: Masquerade, Explained: Why Refusing to Pick a Side Between Two Empires Cost a Korean King His Throne
description: Masquerade (광해, 왕이 된 남자, 2012) imagines a peasant secretly ruling Korea as a body double for King Gwanghaegun — a plot invented entirely for the film. The real Gwanghaegun's story is stranger: a king who tried to keep Joseon out of a war between a collapsing Ming dynasty and a rising Later Jin, whose careful hedging at the 1619 Battle of Sarhu became the pretext for the coup that dethroned him in 1623.
era: Joseon (early 17th century)

title: Gyebaek, Explained: The Mireuksa Gold Plate That Named a Different Queen Than Seonhwa
description: In 2009, workers taking apart the west stone pagoda at Mireuksa in Iksan found a gold plate dated 639. It records that the queen of Baekje who built the monastery was the daughter of Sataek Jeokdeok. The thirteenth-century Samguk yusa says it was Princess Seonhwa of Silla. Here is what the inscription confirms, what it leaves open, and how MBC's Gyebaek (2011) placed both women.
era: Three Kingdoms — Baekje under King Mu (r. 600–641); the Mireuksa gold plate is dated 639

title: Gyeongseong Creature, Explained: The Real Human Experiments Behind the Monster — Unit 731
description: In Netflix's Gyeongseong Creature, the monster is born in a hospital basement where Japanese military doctors treat Korean prisoners as experimental material. The creature is fiction. The experiments it stands for are not: Japan's Unit 731 really did infect prisoners with plague and cholera, really did perform vivisections on living people — and its leaders were never tried, because the U.S. wanted their data. Here's where the drama's horror ends and the documented history begins.
era: Colonial Korea and wartime Manchuria, 1930s–1945 — and the impunity after

title: Three Hun, Seven Po, and Four Mitama: How East Asia Divided the Soul
description: Korea split the person into hon and baek and sent each half to a different address. China counted three hun and seven po. Shintō divided a spirit into functions. Greece sent one soul on one journey. The same inheritance, four different arrangements.
drama: Companion piece to the honbaek post — anchored on Wicked World (멋진 신세계, SBS, 2026)
era: Comparative — Joseon Korea · China · Japan · the Greek and Christian inheritance

title: Wicked World, Explained: Why Joseon Koreans Believed a Dead Person Split in Two
description: SBS's Wicked World opens with Kang Dan-sim hurling away a cup of royal poison, drinking it, and waking centuries later in another woman's body. The body-swap is fantasy. The idea underneath it is not: Joseon's Confucian funeral system described a person as coming apart at death into hon and baek, and gave each half a different ritual destination.
era: Joseon Dynasty (1392–1910) — Confucian funerary and ancestral ritual

title: Undercover Miss Hong, Explained: How Joseon Korea Proved You Were Who You Said You Were
description: In tvN's Undercover Miss Hong, a financial regulator named Hong Geum-bo becomes twenty-year-old Hong Jang-mi and walks into a brokerage. Joseon spent more than 250 years trying to make that impossible with a carried tag called the hopae — introducing it, abandoning it, and starting again. Here is why it kept failing.
era: Joseon Dynasty (1392–1910)

title: Before Passports: How Joseon Korea, Ming China and Tokugawa Japan Proved Who You Were
description: Korea gave you a tag to carry. China gave you a permit to travel and a neighbour to answer for you. Japan made your parish temple vouch for you. Three states, one problem — and none of the answers was built to help you prove anything.
drama: Companion piece to the hopae post — anchored on Undercover Miss Hong (언더커버 미쓰홍, tvN, 2026)
era: Joseon Korea · Ming China · Tokugawa Japan (1603–1867)

title: How Korea Built Universal Health Insurance in 12 Years: Hospital Playlist and the Medical Paradox
description: In Hospital Playlist, Seoul's top doctors work through the night while patients flood in from across the country. Here's the real history behind that scene — from Korea's 1977 workplace insurance law to the 1989 universal-coverage milestone and the 2000 single-payer merger — and how Korea's hybrid system compares with the NHS, American private insurance, and Japan's social-insurance model.
era: Contemporary South Korea (with roots in 1977–1989 healthcare policy)

title: Hotel del Luna, Explained: Why Korean Ghosts Check In Before Moving On
description: In Hotel del Luna (streaming on Netflix), the dead don't simply haunt — they check in to a luxury hotel to untie the grief that keeps them stuck. That premise rests on a centuries-old Korean ritual imagination around the oldest human question: what do we owe the dead? Here's the han, the shamanic gut ritual, and why Korea, China, Japan, and Mexico tend their dead while modern Western horror tends to fear them.
era: Korean folk belief, shamanism & Confucian ritual (modern-day setting)

title: Did Hangul Borrow From the Mongols' Phags-pa Script? What the Evidence Actually Says
description: Did the Mongols' Phags-pa script influence Hangul? We read the Veritable Records, the Hunminjeongeum Haerye and the Yuan edict against each other — and set the Cherokee syllabary alongside them — to separate what the evidence shows from what the theory adds.
drama: Companion to Tree with Deep Roots (뿌리깊은 나무, 2011, SBS) — this piece does not retell the drama; it follows a question the drama leaves open.
era: Yuan and early Joseon, with a nineteenth-century American comparison — Phags-pa promulgated 1269, Hunminjeongeum created 1443 and promulgated 1446, the Cherokee syllabary released 1821

title: Were Gisaeng Like Geisha? Hwang Jini and the Real History Behind Joseon's Female Entertainers
description: In the KBS drama Hwang Jini, a low-caste entertainer trades poems with the greatest scholars of her age. Here's the real history — how Joseon's government-trained artist-courtesans were officially the lowest caste yet received the finest cultural education, and how they compare with Japan's geisha, France's courtesans, and India's tawaif.
era: Mid-Joseon Dynasty (16th century)

show: Once Upon a Time in a Battlefield
title: Once Upon a Time in a Battlefield, Explained: Could Gyebaek and Kim Yu-sin Understand Each Other?
description: In the 2003 satire Once Upon a Time in a Battlefield (황산벌) — described here after the Korean history script this article works from, not screen-checked on our side — Baekje and Silla troops curse at each other in modern Korean regional dialects. Did people of Korea's Three Kingdoms actually need interpreters, and what can the records establish?
drama: Once Upon a Time in a Battlefield (황산벌, 2003, dir. Lee Joon-ik)
era: Three Kingdoms period — the Battle of Hwangsanbeol (660)
tags: Once Upon a Time in a Battlefield

title: Hwarang, Explained: How Silla's Bone-Rank System Shaped Whom You Could Marry, What You Could Wear and Who You Could Become
description: In KBS's Hwarang, five young men train side by side in the same uniform — and the wall between them isn't talent, it's birth. That wall was real. Silla ranked its capital elite by 'bone rank' (golpum): a hereditary grade that shaped whom you could marry, how high you could rise through the seventeen office ranks, what colour your court robes could be, and eventually even the size of your house. Here's how the system actually worked — and what the hwarang were and weren't.
drama: Hwarang: The Poet Warrior Youth (화랑, KBS2, 20 episodes, 2016–2017 · Rakuten Viki in select regions)
era: Silla under King Jinheung, mid-6th century — the bone-rank order

title: Jing-bi-rok, Explained: Why King Seonjo Fled Seoul Before the Palaces Burned
description: In KBS1's Jing-bi-rok, King Seonjo leaves his own capital as the Japanese army closes in — and after he is gone, before the invaders arrive, Seoul's palace offices burn. Here is what the record actually says about Korea's most argued-over royal flight, and how other rulers who lost their capitals were judged.
era: Joseon Dynasty — the Imjin War (1592–1598)

title: Queen Inhyeon and Catherine of Aragon, Explained: Why a Queen's Fall Could Shake an Entire Kingdom
description: In Jang Ok-jung, Living in Love (2013 SBS), Queen Inhyeon is cast out of the palace so a royal favorite can rise. The same drama of a set-aside queen played out in Tudor England with Catherine of Aragon and Henry VIII — but Catherine's fall helped spark the English Reformation, while Inhyeon's triggered Joseon's hwanguk factional purges. Here's the real history of two queens, two kingdoms, and why losing a queen was never a private affair.
drama: Jang Ok-jung, Living in Love (장옥정, 사랑에 살다, SBS, 2013)
era: Joseon (late 17th c.) · Tudor England (16th c.)

title: Why Did Silla Turn on Jang Bogo? Cheonghaejin and What the Records Actually Say
description: KBS's Emperor of the Sea opens with a boy of unfree status on an island, and ends 51 episodes later with a man who made a king. The records are stranger than the drama. Silla did not send Jang Bogo to command the sea — he already commanded it, and the court ratified what already existed. Thirteen to eighteen years later — the sources disagree on the year — the same court sent a man to kill him, and in 851, twenty-three years after the garrison was founded, it abolished Cheonghaejin itself. This article follows what the sources actually say, including the parts where they contradict each other: the Samguk Sagi puts his death in 846, a Japanese chronicle puts it in November 841, and the twelfth-century compiler who noticed the gap refused to close it.
drama: Emperor of the Sea (해신, KBS2, 24 November 2004 – 25 May 2005, 51 episodes) — a historical epic based on Choi In-ho's 2003 novel Haesin, starring Choi Soo-jong as Gungbok/Jang Bogo, Chae Shi-ra, Song Il-kook as Yeomjang and Soo Ae
era: Unified Silla — Cheonghaejin established in 828 under King Heungdeok and abolished in the second month of 851 under King Munseong

title: The Book of Fish, Explained: Jeong Yak-jeon, the Jasaneobo, and Korea's Forgotten Naturalist
description: In the 2021 Korean film The Book of Fish (자산어보, released in Korea as Jasan Fish), the Silhak scholar Jeong Yak-jeon arrives at a remote island as a political exile and — sixteen years later — leaves it only in death, having catalogued the marine life of the Heuksan waters into 55 categories with the help of a local islander. Here is the real story of the Jasaneobo, Joseon's most remarkable natural history text, and how it sits alongside Li Shizhen's Bencao Gangmu and Alexander von Humboldt in the global story of observational science.
drama: The Book of Fish (자산어보 / Jasan Fish, 2021, Megabox Plus M)
era: Late Joseon Korea — the Silhak period (early 19th century)

show: Two anchors rather than one: The East Palace
title: What Actually Changed When Western Medicine Reached Korea? The 1886 Jejungwon Report
description: Korean court dramas move from palace curse cases to a Western hospital in a single generation, and the story usually gets told as belief giving way to science. The documents support something narrower and more checkable. In 1886 two doctors filed a first-year report on the Korean government's new hospital. It is a registered cultural property; summaries of it describe 10,460 patients, set out in the disease categories of Western medicine. What we can actually document changing first is not what Koreans believed about illness, but what got written down — and we mark clearly which parts of that report we confirmed and which we did not.
drama: Two anchors rather than one: The East Palace (동궁, 2026, Netflix), which turns on a court curse case, and Jejungwon (제중원, 2010, SBS), set at Korea's first government Western hospital in 1885–86. Roughly three centuries separate the worlds they depict.
era: Late Joseon and the opening of Korea — Gwanghyewon opens in April 1885 and is renamed Jejungwon the same month; the first-year report is filed in 1886

title: SBS's Jejungwon: The True Story of Korea's First Government Western Hospital
description: SBS's Jejungwon was based on a real government hospital. After Horace Allen treated Min Yeong-ik's sword wounds during the 1884 Gapsin Coup, Joseon opened Gwanghyewon — renamed Jejungwon weeks later. Here is what the drama compresses, and why the claim that it produced Korea's first Western-trained doctors is not quite right.
era: Joseon Dynasty — 1884–1886, the dawn of Korea's opening to Western medicine

title: Jeong Do-jeon, Explained: Could a Powerful Chief Minister Protect Joseon From a Bad King?
description: In KBS1's sweeping 2014 epic Jeong Do-jeon, the scholar who designed the Joseon dynasty argues that a capable chief minister — not the king alone — should run the country day to day. It's a real 14th-century political design that cost him his life, and scholars still disagree about what he actually meant by it.
drama: Jeong Do-jeon (정도전, KBS1, 50 episodes, 4 Jan – 29 Jun 2014)
era: Late Goryeo–early Joseon transition, c. 1392–1398

show: Lee San, Wind of the Palace
title: MBC's Lee San, Explained: What 'I Am the Son of Crown Prince Sado' Really Meant
description: When Lee San's King Jeongjo says 'I am the son of Crown Prince Sado' on the day he takes the throne, it plays like a son's grief. In real Joseon history it was grief, an acceptance of the succession order — and a warning. Here's the 24-year reign that followed: a library, a fortress city, a royal guard, and 297 secret letters to his own rival.
drama: Lee San, Wind of the Palace (이산, MBC, 77 episodes, 2007–2008)
era: Joseon Dynasty — reign of King Jeongjo, 1776–1800

title: Brothers in 1627, Sovereign and Subject Demanded in 1636 — The War Before The Fortress, Explained
description: The Fortress (남한산성, 2017) opens in the winter of 1636 and never leaves the 47 days inside the walls. Nine years before that winter, Joseon and the Later Jin had already fought a war and already sworn a peace, and that settlement was framed as a covenant between brother states. This article follows what the 1627 settlement actually said, where the records disagree about when that war ended, and how a relationship of brothers was demanded back as one of sovereign and subject — working from the Annals of King Injo, the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture and Urihistorynet, and marking the places where it could not collate the original.
drama: The Fortress (남한산성, 2017, dir. Hwang Dong-hyuk, adapted from Kim Hoon's novel; Lee Byung-hun as Choi Myung-gil, Kim Yoon-seok as Kim Sang-heon, Park Hae-il as King Injo, Heo Sung-tae as Yonggoldae)
era: Joseon Korea, 1627–1636 — from the Later Jin invasion known as the Jeongmyo horan to the eve of the Qing invasion the film depicts

title: What Is Yeoseong Gukgeuk? Jeong Nyeon & Korea's Lost All-Female Theater, Explained
description: In Jeong Nyeon, the stage of 1950s Seoul belongs entirely to women — playing warriors, kings, and lovers to screaming female fans. Here's the real history of yeoseong gukgeuk, the all-female theatrical genre that exploded after the Korean War, how it compared with Japan's Takarazuka Revue and Shakespeare's all-male London stage, and why it vanished — and how Jeong Nyeon (2024, MBC) helped bring it back.
era: Post-Korean War South Korea (late 1940s–1960s)

show: Because This Is My First Life
title: Because This Is My First Life, Explained: Why Ji-ho Is Sent to the Kitchen During Jesa
description: In Because This Is My First Life, a new bride is handed an apron the moment she walks into her in-laws' ancestral rite. Here is what jesa actually is, what jongbeop did and did not decide, why the eldest-son version is younger than most people assume — and how five traditions answered the same question about what the living owe the dead.
drama: Because This Is My First Life (이번 생은 처음이라, tvN, 2017)
era: Late Goryeo through Joseon (1392–1910) and contemporary South Korea
tags: Because This Is My First Life

title: Battle of Jinpo 1380: How Choe Museon Gave Goryeo Its Own Gunpowder — The History Behind Six Flying Dragons
description: Six Flying Dragons opens in the last years of Goryeo and spends fifty episodes on how a dynasty is ended in council rooms. It does not show the autumn of 1380, when a Goryeo fleet sailed into the Geum estuary carrying a weapon the kingdom had only just learned to make. This article follows the man who spent years asking merchants for one recipe — saltpetre — and puts the surviving records of Jinpo next to the popular telling: what the sources say about tied-together ships, what they don't say about ranges and weapons, and why 'the world's first naval gunpowder battle' is a claim the evidence cannot carry.
drama: Six Flying Dragons (육룡이 나르샤, SBS, 2015–2016, 50 episodes) — a political drama about the founding of Joseon, centred on Yi Bang-won, Jeong Do-jeon and Yi Seong-gye
era: Late Goryeo — reign of King U (1374–1388); the Hwatong Dogam is founded in 1377 and the Battle of Jinpo is fought in the eighth lunar month of 1380

title: Joseon Divorce Law: Seven Grounds, Three Exceptions
description: Joseon Attorney raises the question: how did divorce work? Not every yangban needed the king's permission, but investigated cases went to the king, as in the 1440 case of Yi Maeng-gyun's wife.
era: Joseon Dynasty (1392–1910)

title: Curse, Ritual, or Contagion? How Joseon Explained and Responded to Illness
description: The East Palace answers a crown prince's death with an exorcist; Jejungwon answers illness with a Western hospital. Between them sits a documented Joseon state that held an official rite for the dead who received no sacrifice, ordered magistrates in 1429 to use physicians and shamans together, and printed a plague manual in the Korean alphabet in 1525. This article sets out what each record shows, and keeps responses and explanations apart.
drama: Two anchors: The East Palace (동궁, Netflix, 2026, 8 episodes; Cho Seung-woo, Nam Joo-hyuk, Roh Yoon-seo) — an occult period drama set in an invented dynasty — and Jejungwon (제중원, SBS, 2010, 36 episodes), set at the Western-style government hospital Joseon opened in 1885. Jejungwon's current international streaming could not be confirmed; The East Palace is a Netflix original. The dramas' ghosts, exorcist, medium and fictional students are fiction and are not fact-checked here.
era: Joseon, 1401–1908 — from the founding of the state rite for the unsacrificed dead to its formal abolition

title: Six Flying Dragons and My Royal Nemesis, Explained: How Joseon Korea Actually Decided a Death Sentence
description: A cup of royal poison in one drama, a sword to the neck in another. Both point at real Joseon punishment — but not in the way the shows suggest. Here is the Daemyeongnyul, the Five Punishments, what sayak actually was, and what really set a sentence.
drama: My Royal Nemesis (멋진 신세계, SBS, 2026) · Six Flying Dragons (육룡이 나르샤, SBS, 2015–2016)
era: Joseon Dynasty founding era (1388–1398); Daemyeongnyul-based penal system, 1395–1905

title: Joseon Fire Service Explained: Geumhwadogam, Myeolhwagun, and the 1426 Hanyang Fire
description: In 1426 the capital burned while the king was away hunting. What Joseon built afterwards was not a hero but an office: the Geumhwadogam, firebreaks and wells, axe-carrying crews, bell signals — and, written into the regulations, palace-office women assigned to carry water to the fire.
drama: The Great King, Sejong (대왕 세종, KBS, 2008)
era: Joseon — Sejong's reign, the great fire of 1426

title: Notes from the Last Row: The Joseon History of Ghostwriting, Daejak, and Exam Fraud
description: A family could pay a famous stylist to write a father's epitaph and nobody pretended otherwise. Carry the same act into the examination hall and it became a crime against the state. Joseon had no copyright regime comparable to modern authors' rights — what it policed was not authorship but the gate.
drama: Notes from the Last Row (맨 끝줄 소년, Netflix, 2026)
era: Joseon Dynasty (1392–1897), with Goryeo precedents from 1062 onward

title: Mr. Kim, Explained: If Your Daughter Vanished in Joseon Korea, Who Would Look for Her?
description: In SBS's Mr. Kim, a father takes a call from his missing daughter's number in a police station and detectives stop him. He walks out and looks for her himself. Joseon Korea had real police, real forensics and real courts — but no documented office that opened a file on a person who simply did not come home. Here is what the records actually show, and who did the looking instead.
era: Joseon dynasty (1392–1897)

title: What Was a Daegunbuin? Perfect Crown and How Joseon Filed Its Royal Women
description: In Joseon, a daegun's wife was a bubuin, not a gunbuin. MBC's Perfect Crown uses the second word and Korean viewers noticed. The error is not a demotion by one grade — the two titles could sit at the same rank — but a wrong category. Here is the ladder of Joseon royal women's titles: gongju, ongju, bubuin, gunbuin, naemyeongbu and oemyeongbu.
era: Joseon

title: Rookie Historian Goo Hae-ryung, Explained: Could Joseon's Historians Record What the King Wanted Hidden?
description: In Rookie Historian Goo Hae-ryung (신입사관 구해령, 2019), a young woman fights to become a court historian. Female historians were fiction — but the job itself was one of the most powerful in Joseon. When King Taejong fell off his horse and said 'don't let the historians know,' the historians wrote down that too. Here's how Joseon's record-keepers compared to China's, Japan's, and the West's.
drama: Rookie Historian Goo Hae-ryung (신입사관 구해령, 2019 MBC)
era: Joseon Dynasty (1392–1910)

title: Did the Joseon Government Pay for Weddings? What the Royal Records Actually Say
description: Yes, in some cases. Joseon records show the state giving grain or wedding goods when poverty delayed marriage, from a 1472 order for poor women aged 25 and over to a law for poor sajok daughters nearing thirty, but no standing agency that assigned spouses to every unmarried person.
drama: Flower Crew: Joseon Marriage Agency (조선혼담공작소 꽃파당, JTBC, 2019, 16 episodes). This article discusses the drama's general premise, not specific episodes. The drama has been listed on Viki and other services, but availability varies by country and region, and current official availability was not confirmed
era: Joseon. Mainly the reigns of Taejong (1414), Sejong (1427–1440), Seongjong (1472–1491) and Jeongjo (1791), with the Gyeongguk daejeon and the Sokdaejeon. Brief comparison with Zhu Xi's Family Rituals, Augustan Rome and Fascist Italy

title: Jing-bi-rok, Explained: How Korea and Japan Went from Seven Years of War to Two Centuries of Tongsinsa Diplomacy
description: In KBS1's Jing-bi-rok, two Joseon envoys come home from Japan in 1591 with opposite verdicts on Toyotomi Hideyoshi — and the Imjin War follows. What the drama doesn't show is the stranger sequel: after seven years of war, Korea and Japan built a diplomatic relationship that lasted two hundred years and twelve embassies.
era: Joseon Dynasty — the 1590–91 mission to Japan through the Tongsinsa embassies of 1607–1811

title: Flower Crew: Joseon Marriage Agency, Explained: Why Joseon Marriage Was a Family Affair, Not Just a Love Story
description: In Flower Crew: Joseon Marriage Agency, a fictional matchmaking firm stages a king's wedding — and the groom vanishes before the ceremony ends. Here's the real machinery behind a Joseon marriage: matchmakers, birth-chart paperwork, a mysterious wooden box, and why Joseon, China, Europe, and India all treated marriage as a matter of families, not just two people.
drama: Flower Crew: Joseon Marriage Agency (꽃파당: 조선혼담공작소, 2019 JTBC)
era: Joseon Dynasty — fictional reign; customs shown reflect general Joseon-era practice (1392–1910)

title: Netflix's Mr. Sunshine, Explained: Why Joseon Never Bound Its Women's Feet — and What It Controlled Instead
description: In Netflix's Mr. Sunshine, noblewoman Go Ae-shin sprints across rooftops and fires a rifle without her hanbok ever slowing her down. Korea never adopted China's foot-binding — but that's not the same as saying Joseon women were free, and this piece is careful not to blur the two.
era: Joseon Dynasty (1392–1910); the drama is set in the 1900s, during the Righteous Army resistance

title: Under the Queen's Umbrella, Explained: Why Joseon Women Had Names — But History Often Erased Them
description: In tvN's Under the Queen's Umbrella, royal concubines are addressed only by court rank — 숙용, 소용, 귀인 — never by a personal name. That's not just palace formality: even famous Joseon women, like Shin Saimdang, often left no birth name in the official record at all. Here's why.
era: Joseon

title: Jumong, Explained: Why the Records Tell Different Stories of Goguryeo's Founder
description: The drama shows a prince driven out of Buyeo who builds a kingdom in exile. That is one surviving version. The oldest Goguryeo record of its own founder does not mention the persecution at all, and one tradition has him inherit a throne rather than lose one.
drama: Ju Mong, Prince of Legend (주몽, MBC, 2006–2007, 81 episodes)
era: Goguryeo — the founding traditions, 1st century BCE

title: My Dearest, Explained: Who Were the Karayuki-san — and Why They Weren't the Japanese Military's 'Comfort Women'
description: MBC's My Dearest (연인, 2023) follows the hwanghyangnyeo — Joseon women taken captive in the 1636–37 Qing war and shamed on their return. That story is often, wrongly, folded into others: the Japanese military's 'comfort women,' and the little-known Karayuki-san, poor Japanese women sold abroad in the Meiji era. Here's who the Karayuki-san actually were, and why keeping these three histories apart matters.
era: Meiji–Taishō Japan (late 19th–early 20th c.), with a Joseon (17th c.) point of comparison

title: Kim Man-deok, Explained: How a Former Gisaeng Became Jeju's Legendary Merchant
description: The 2010 KBS drama 거상 김만덕 tells the story of a Jeju woman who rose from the gisaeng registry to become one of Joseon's wealthiest merchants — then gave much of it away in a famine. Here's the real history: her petition to reclaim commoner status, the 1794–95 Jeju famine, and the almost unheard-of royal reward King Jeongjo granted her.
drama: The Great Merchant Kim Man-deok (거상 김만덕, KBS, 2010)
era: Joseon dynasty, reign of King Jeongjo (18th century)

title: Netflix's Kingdom, Explained: Why Hunger, Not Zombies, Is the Real Monster
description: In Netflix's Kingdom, starving peasants turn into something terrifying. But here's what the show is really about: in Joseon Korea, famine wasn't just a disaster — it was a verdict on the king himself. And the way five civilizations read hunger tells you everything about how they believed the world worked.
era: Joseon Dynasty — set c. 1601, just after the Imjin War

title: Netflix's The King's Affection, Explained: Why a Joseon Prince Punched a Ming Envoy Over a Haircut
description: In The King's Affection, Yi Hwi punches a Ming envoy for cutting a court lady's hair — and many Korean viewers cheered. Here's the 2,000-year-old idea about hair behind it, what 'sadae' really meant, and how cutting hair carried wildly different meanings across the world.
era: Joseon Dynasty (1392–1910)

show: Guardian: The Lonely and Great God
title: Why the Korean Grim Reaper Wears a Black Hat — and Why It Isn't an Ancient Tradition
description: In Guardian: The Lonely and Great God (도깨비), Hotel del Luna, and Along with the Gods, death arrives as a calm man in a black hat and coat — the jeoseung-saja. But the black-hatted reaper isn't from old scripture. Here's where the look really comes from, and why the Korean death-messenger is closer to a civil servant than a monster.
drama: Guardian: The Lonely and Great God (도깨비, 2016), Hotel del Luna (호텔 델루나, 2019) & Along with the Gods (신과 함께, 2017)
era: Korean Buddhist & folk afterlife tradition

title: MAL·MO·E, Explained: Korea's Dictionary Was a Crime — and the Woman at the Centre of the Famous Origin Story Said It Wasn't True
description: In MAL·MO·E: The Secret Mission (말모이, 2019), scholars compile a Korean dictionary in a bookshop basement until the police come. The film invents an informant. Popular history invents a schoolgirl's diary. In 1998 the schoolgirl herself sat down with Korea's National Institute of Korean Language and said the diary story was wrong. What the colonial court actually wrote down is stranger — and wider — than either version.
drama: MAL·MO·E: The Secret Mission (말모이, 2019, dir. Eom Yu-na) — set in the early 1940s, around the Korean Language Society incident of 1942
era: Japanese colonial period — the Korean Language Society incident, 1942–1945

title: Misaeng Explained: Korea's Contract Worker Crisis, the IMF Era, and the Two-Year Rule
description: In Misaeng (미생), Jang Geu-rae survives inside a giant corporation as a lowly contract worker. Here's what his fear really means — Korea's non-regular employment crisis born after the 1997 IMF shock — and how Japan, China, and America each grew their own version of the same anxiety.
era: Contemporary South Korea

title: Netflix's The Moon Embracing the Sun, Explained: Why a Confucian Kingdom Still Needed Its Shamans
description: In Netflix's The Moon Embracing the Sun, a court shaman moves through a kingdom that officially called shamanism a superstition. Here's why Confucian Joseon never managed to be rid of its mudang — and how Korea, China, Japan, and the West each handled the magic their official order disapproved of.
drama: The Moon Embracing the Sun (해를 품은 달, 2012)
era: Joseon Dynasty (1392–1910)

title: Mousetrap, Explained: The Rat Knew the House Better Than the Son
description: Netflix's Mousetrap (들쥐, 2026) starts from a Korean oral folktale in which a rat eats a man's discarded nail clippings and takes his place — and in the version recorded at Yeongdong in 1982 the horror is not the transformation but the parents who test the two men on household knowledge and pick the rat. This article works from a 1982 field recording made in Yeongdong, the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture entries on the tale and on the classical novel Ongojipjeon, Netflix's official episode descriptions and press release, and two published director interviews. It did not collate the drama's video or Korean subtitles at any point, and it marks which scene details rest only on episode reviews.
drama: Mousetrap (들쥐, 2026, Netflix, 10 episodes, released 28 August 2026, dir. Kim Hong-sun, written by Lee Jae-gon, based on the Kakao Webtoon of the same name by Ludvico)
era: Korean oral folktale tradition — the version discussed here was recorded in the field in 1982 — and the classical novel Ongojipjeon, whose author and date are unknown; the drama itself is contemporary

title: Netflix's Mr. Queen, Explained: Why Does Korea Have So Many Kims?
description: Joseon had so many powerful Kims because in the 1800s a few royal in-law clans, above all the Andong Kim, ruled through sedo politics — marrying their daughters to boy-kings and packing the government with kinsmen. Korea has so many Kims overall because surnames began as an elite privilege and spread to everyone over centuries; the bon-gwan (ancestral clan seat) tells unrelated Kims apart. Netflix's Mr. Queen makes its heroine an Andong Kim.
era: Joseon dynasty (1392–1897)

title: Mr. Sunshine, Revisited: Why Baekjeong Stigma Faded in Korea but Burakumin Discrimination Survived in Japan
description: Korea and Japan both abolished their hereditary outcast classes — Korea's baekjeong in 1894, Japan's burakumin in 1871. A century later the results split sharply: in Korea the stigma faded, while Japan needed a new anti-discrimination law as recently as 2016. Here's the real reason — not morality, but traceability: who could still be tracked back to an outcast bloodline, through household registers, address books, and a secret 1975 list of 5,300 villages.
era: Late Joseon to the present (1894–2016)

title: Netflix's Mr. Sunshine, Explained: Why the Butcher's Son Could Never Escape His Blood
description: In Mr. Sunshine, Gu Dong-mae is brilliant, feared, and powerful — yet one word, 'butcher,' follows him everywhere. Here's what a baekjeong really was in Joseon Korea, why blood and leather marked a person for life, and how Korea, Japan, India, and medieval Europe each built almost the same untouchable class out of the same idea.
era: Late Joseon / Korean Empire

title: Why Was Korea's Righteous Army Called a \"Mob\"? The Real History Behind Mr. Sunshine
description: Japanese army records called Korea's Righteous Army (의병, uibyeong) pokdo (暴徒), \"rioters\" — the word even heads the title of the garrison army's own campaign history. Its commander Yi In-yeong asked foreign consulates to recognize it as a belligerent body: the real history behind Mr. Sunshine (tvN, 2018).
era: Korean Empire (1897–1910) — the Righteous Army resistance of 1907–1910

title: Exhuma, Explained: A Baekje King Bought His Burial Plot From the Powers Below — and the Deed Survived 1,500 Years
description: In Exhuma (파묘, 2024), people shout at the ground before they break it and a geomancer tastes the soil. Fifteen centuries earlier a Baekje king dealt with the same problem in writing. The most remarkable object from the tomb of King Muryeong is not a gold ornament but a stone slab carrying a maejigwon — a funerary deed that borrows the form of a land sale, names earth deities and the officials of the world below as the other party, records a price, and was buried with iron coins on the same stone. It is the only royal tomb of Korea's Three Kingdoms whose occupant is confirmed by name.
drama: Exhuma (파묘, 2024, dir. Jang Jae-hyun) — a shaman-and-geomancer occult film built around the disturbing of a grave
era: Three Kingdoms — Baekje, the Ungjin period; King Muryeong r. 501–523, tomb deed dated 525

title: Age of Warriors (무인시대), Explained: The Slap That Didn't Cause Goryeo's Military Coup
description: KBS1's 158-episode epic opens with a courtier slapping a general, and a century of military rule follows. The slap is real. But the coup was already planned before the hand came down. Here's what actually drove Goryeo's generals to take the government — and why only one of them died in his own bed.
era: Goryeo Dynasty — the 1170 coup and the military regime (1170–1270)

title: Our Blooming Youth, Explained: Why Joseon Korea Had a Forensics Manual Centuries Before Sherlock Holmes
description: In tvN's Our Blooming Youth, the leads solve deaths with evidence, not superstition — and that's not artistic license. Here's the real history behind it: the Muwonrok, Joseon Korea's official death-investigation manual, its Chinese and Mongol-dynasty roots, the dual-inquest system built to catch corrupt magistrates, and the low-status corpse handlers who actually did the forensic work.
era: Joseon dynasty (1392–1897)

title: My Dearest, Explained: Why Joseon Punished the Women It Failed to Protect
description: In My Dearest (연인), women dragged off as war captives return home — only to be shamed by their own families. Here's the real history of the hwanhyangnyeo after the 1636 Qing invasion, the chastity ideology behind it, and how France did something hauntingly similar in 1945.
era: Joseon Dynasty (Qing invasion, 1636–37)

title: Why Did Joseon Koreans Believe a King's Grave Could Change Dynasties? Geomancy, Physiognomy, and the Politics of Fate, Explained
description: In Myeongdang and The Face Reader, a grave site and a glance at someone's eyes carry the weight of dynastic fate. Here's the real history — from Goryeo's state geomancy decrees to Joseon's official Bureau of Astronomy and Geomancy, the grave-theft lawsuits that filled the royal annals, and how Korea's tradition of reading land and faces compares with China's feng shui, India's Vastu Shastra, and Western phrenology.
drama: Myeongdang (명당, 2018, Lotte Entertainment) & The Face Reader (관상, 2013, CJ Entertainment)
era: Goryeo and Joseon Dynasties (918–1897)

title: How Did 12 Ships Hold Off a Fleet of 133? Yi Sun-sin and the Battle of Myeongnyang, Explained
description: In the 2014 blockbuster The Admiral: Roaring Currents (명량), Yi Sun-sin faces the worst odds in Korean military history — 12 panokseon against a Japanese fleet of 300 ships. Here is the real history of the battle: how a 300-metre strait, a reversing tidal current, and tactical precision turned naval arithmetic on its head — and what the film gets right, what it disputes, and what it invents.
drama: The Admiral: Roaring Currents (명량, 2014, CJ ENM)
era: Late Joseon Korea — the Imjin War period (1592–1598)

title: KBS's Empress Myeongseong: The True Story of the Eulmi Assassination
description: In 1895, Japanese agents organized by Minister Miura Gorō entered Gyeongbokgung Palace, killed Queen Min, and burned her body. Here is the true history behind KBS's Empress Myeongseong and the Eulmi Incident — including why the Hiroshima case ended without a trial.
era: Late Joseon Dynasty / early Korean Empire — 1895–1897

title: Love in the Moonlight, Explained: Joseon's Court Eunuchs Left Behind a Family Tree With 777 Names
description: In Love in the Moonlight, a woman hides in plain sight as a palace eunuch — a disguise that only works if you picture a eunuch as a man with nothing and no one. Real Joseon naesi had wives, adopted sons, burial plots, and a genealogy book. And the famous theory of why courts trusted eunuchs — no family, no stake — turns out to fail almost everywhere you check it.
drama: Love in the Moonlight (구르미 그린 달빛, 2016 KBS2)
era: Joseon Dynasty (1392–1910)

title: Samjeondo Humiliation, Explained: Why King Injo Submitted to the Qing Emperor
description: In The Fortress (남한산성, 2017), the Joseon king endures 47 days of siege before descending to perform the sambaegugo-du — three bows, nine prostrations — before the Qing emperor. Here's the real history behind the Manchu invasion of 1636, the ideological split that paralyzed Joseon's court, and how Korea's most painful act of submission compares with the Walk to Canossa, East Asia's tribute system, and the modern grammar of surrender.
era: Late Joseon, Byeongjahoran (Manchu Invasion of Korea, 1636–1637)

title: Feng Shui (Myeongdang), Explained: Did Namyeongun's Tomb Really Make Gojong King?
description: No — the Namyeongun tomb did not make Gojong king; that is feng-shui legend, not established cause and effect. What is documented: Heungseon Daewongun moved his father's grave to the foot of Gayasan in 1846, and after King Cheoljong died without an heir in 1863, Queen Dowager Sinjeong chose his son Myeongbok, later King Gojong. The film Myeongdang (Feng Shui) asks whether a burial site can change a family's destiny; here's what's history, what's legend, and why the line matters.
era: Joseon Dynasty (1392–1910)

title: Why Did Korea's Farmers Take Up Bamboo Spears? Nokdu Flower and the Donghak Peasant Revolution, Explained
description: In SBS's 2019 drama Nokdu Flower (녹두꽃), peasant farmers sign a circular petition, seize a county office, and march against a corrupt magistrate — launching what becomes Korea's largest pre-modern uprising. Here is the real history: the Donghak religion turned revolutionary movement, the sabal tongmun, the Jipgangso self-governance experiment, and why the 1894 peasant revolt became a decisive trigger of the First Sino-Japanese War.
era: Late Joseon Korea (1894) — the Donghak Peasant Revolution

title: Nongae, Explained: Did a Gisaeng Really Pull a Japanese Commander to His Death at Jinju?
description: Sageuk about the Imjin War keep returning to one scene from the 1593 fall of Jinju: Nongae, a Joseon woman, luring a Japanese commander onto a rock above the river and leaping in with him. Here's the real history behind the legend — where it comes from, why a gisaeng waited 150 years for the state to honor her, and why calling her 'Korea's Joan of Arc' both fits and misleads.
era: Joseon — the Imjin War (1592–1598), Jinju fell in 1593

title: The Ming Commanders Who Fought From Korean Ships — Noryang, Yi Sun-sin's Last Battle, Explained
description: In Noryang: Deadly Sea (2023), the conflict the film puts up front is between Yi Sun-sin and the Ming admiral Chen Lin. Behind that conflict the records preserve a detail the film's published synopsis does not mention: at the last large naval battle of the Imjin War, Ming commanders fought from Korean panokseon warships. Two sources of different kinds — the Joseon court annals and Shin Heum's private collection, the Sangchonjip — describe Ming officers on Korean decks, and both name the Ming commander-in-chief Chen Lin among them, though this article does not claim the two are textually independent of each other. Here is what those records actually say, including the places where they disagree with each other.
drama: Noryang: Deadly Sea (노량: 죽음의 바다, 2023, dir. Kim Han-min)
era: Joseon Korea — the closing days of the Imjin War (1598)

title: Minari, Explained: Why the Family Sleeps on the Floor — and What Ondol Has to Do With It
description: Why does the family in Minari sleep on the floor? There is no ondol in the Arkansas trailer — no firebox, no flue, no heated stone — and yet the floor is where they end up. This article follows Korea's underfloor heating from a line in a Chinese dynastic history about what poor people did in winter, through the late arrival of the fully heated room, to the habits it left in the body: shoes at the threshold, low furniture, and the warmest spot in the room given to the eldest.
drama: Minari (미나리, 2020, dir. Lee Isaac Chung, A24, 115 minutes) — a semi-autobiographical film drawn from Chung's own childhood, following a Korean immigrant family who leave California for a plot of land in rural Arkansas in the 1980s. Youn Yuh-jung, who plays the grandmother Soon-ja, won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress. Where and how it streams differs by country and changes often, so this article does not state it.
era: Long span — the earliest partial-floor heating is dated by the Korea Heritage Service to the 4th century BCE–1st century CE; the fully heated room is generally placed in late Goryeo; the most active period of installation is the 17th century

title: Are the Haenyeo in Our Blues & When Life Gives You Tangerines Real? Jeju's Diving Grandmothers, Explained
description: Our Blues and When Life Gives You Tangerines both put Jeju's haenyeo on screen — women in their 60s, 70s, and 80s who dive into the cold sea with no oxygen tank. Here's what the haenyeo really are, why their breath is called a 'sound,' how they built a rare matriarchal labor culture, and how their world compares with Japan's ama and women's fishing labor across the globe.
drama: Our Blues (우리들의 블루스, 2022) & When Life Gives You Tangerines (폭싹 속았수다, 2025)
era: Jeju Island (modern & 20th century)

title: Pachinko, Explained: Why Changing a Name Was a Colonial Wound
description: In Apple TV+'s Pachinko, characters carry Korean names, Japanese names, and family secrets all at once. Here's the real history behind it — Japan's Sōshi-kaimei name-change policy, why a name was never just a label, and how colonial powers from Taiwan to Canada used names as a tool of erasure.
era: Japanese colonial period (1910–1945)

title: Pachinko, Explained: The Korean Women Who Crossed the Pacific With Only a Photograph
description: In Pachinko, Sunja marries a pastor who has lodged in her house for a few weeks and sails to Osaka. Viewers read it as her misfortune. But a generation earlier, from the same coastline, Korean women were crossing a far wider ocean to marry men they had never met at all — a photograph was the whole courtship. Between 1910 and 1924 several hundred to eleven hundred of them landed in Hawaii. The photograph was not a romantic token. It was paperwork. And the empire that issued it was not their own.
drama: Pachinko (파친코, 2022 · season 2, 2024, Apple TV+) — Sunja leaves Yeongdo, Busan for Osaka in the 1930s
era: Japanese colonial period — Korean picture brides to Hawaii, 1910–1924

title: Why Did Korea Send Miners and Nurses to West Germany? Ode to My Father, Explained
description: In Ode to My Father, a young man takes a mining job in West Germany to pay his brother's tuition. The recruitment was real: in 1963, some 46,000 people applied for 500 places. This article separates what the records support from the story Korea has told about it — including the widely repeated claim that the workers' wages were pledged as collateral for a German loan, which a state commission examined and rejected.
drama: Ode to My Father (국제시장, 2014, dir. Yoon Je-kyoon) — a family melodrama that runs from the 1950 Heungnam evacuation to the present, with Hwang Jung-min as Deok-su. The Korean Film Council's KoBiz gives a running time of 126 minutes and cumulative admissions of 14,269,712; the Korean Film Archive's KMDb gives 131 minutes. Where and how it streams differs by country and changes often, so this article does not state it.
era: Post-war and industrialising Korea — miners were sent to West Germany from 1963, nursing staff from the late 1950s privately and from 1966 through state channels

title: Queen Dowager Cheonchu and the 1009 Coup: Why Her Nephew Became King and Her Son Died
description: According to the Goryeosa, Queen Dowager Cheonchu's side tried to push aside her nephew, Prince Daeryangwon, and harm him. In the 1009 coup, that nephew became King Hyeonjong, and the person who died was her son, King Mokjong, killed on the road into exile by men sent by the coup leader Gang Jo. This article follows the Goryeosa, the Goryeosa Jeolyo, a 1006 gold-ink sutra and two epitaphs from the Choe Sa-wi family. It separates what those records say from what they cannot settle, including the fact that the family of one of the coup's winners had already compared her to Empress Lü of Han long before the Goryeosa was compiled.
drama: Korea-Khitan War (고려 거란 전쟁, KBS2, first broadcast November 2023, 2023–2024, 32 episodes). Queen Dowager Cheonchu appears in the early episodes; this article draws on episodes 2–4. The English title is the one used on Netflix's official title page. Availability varies by country, and this article did not confirm which countries carry it
era: Goryeo. The reign of King Mokjong (997–1009), Gang Jo's coup of 1009, and Queen Dowager Cheonchu's life (964–1029). The Khitan invasion of 1010 is mentioned only as background

title: Queen of Tears, Explained: Why Korea's Chaebol Families Are Drawn Like Royal Dynasties
description: In Queen of Tears, the Queens Group family fights over control, marriage, and inheritance as if they were a royal house — not a company. Here's why Korea's chaebol really do behave like dynasties, how a small family controls a giant empire, and why Japan's zaibatsu were dismantled after WWII while Korea's chaebol survived and grew stronger.
era: Contemporary South Korea

title: Queen Seondeok, Explained: How Silla Put a Woman on the Throne in the Seventh Century
description: In MBC's epic Queen Seondeok, an abandoned princess claws her way to the crown past the villainous Mishil. The real story is stranger: Silla crowned Deokman in 632 not because it believed in equality, but because its obsession with sacred royal blood outweighed her sex. Here's what actually made Korea's first female ruler possible — and what the drama invented, including Mishil herself.
drama: The Great Queen Seondeok (선덕여왕, MBC, 62 episodes, 2009 · Rakuten Viki in select regions)
era: Silla, 632–647 — the reign of Korea's first female ruler

title: The Red Sleeve, Explained: Why Did Seong Deok-im Refuse King Jeongjo?
description: Why did Seong Deok-im refuse King Jeongjo — not once but more than once? History says the real woman did too. Here's what a Joseon court lady (gungnyeo) actually was, why a king's favor could close more doors than it opened, and how Korea, China, Japan, the Ottoman Empire, and the West each caged the women of the palace.
era: Joseon Dynasty (1392–1910)

title: Was Reply 1988's Alley Community Real? Yeontan, the Seoul Olympics, and Korea's Compressed Modernization
description: In Reply 1988 (tvN, 2015–2016), five families in a single Seoul alleyway share coal briquettes (yeontan), meals, and childcare as naturally as breathing. Here's the real history behind that neighborly world — Korea's 30-year compressed modernization, the double meaning of the 1988 Seoul Olympics, and the eviction protests the Games left out — and how it compares with postwar America, Europe, and Japan.
era: 1980s South Korea (compressed modernization era)

title: Revenant and Korean Ghost Folklore: How 1960s Cinema Shaped the Woman in White
description: Korean horror films of the mid-1960s helped make the white-clad, loose-haired female ghost a widely recognized visual convention. This article traces that history from Joseon literary descriptions to the cinema, with a short detour into related folklore of the unmarried dead.
drama: Revenant (악귀, 2023, SBS, 12 episodes) — written by Kim Eun-hee, directed by Lee Jung-rim and Kim Jae-hong; starring Kim Tae-ri (Gu San-yeong), Oh Jung-se (Yeom Hae-sang) and Hong Kyung (Lee Hong-sae). Streaming availability varies by region — check the official platform where you are. This article uses only what episode 1 shows and the drama's recurring visual motifs; it does not reveal the revenant's identity or how the story ends.
era: Joseon literature (15th–19th century) to Korean cinema of the 1960s — with folk practice recorded in twentieth-century surveys

title: Rookie Historian, Explained: Why Joseon Never Had a Female Court Historian — and What Women Did Instead
description: No — Joseon Korea had no institutional female court historian (sagwan): all sagwan appointments were male, and women were barred from the civil service examinations. Real sagwan kept candid daily drafts (sacho) of the king that were compiled into the UNESCO-listed Veritable Records (Sillok), and women instead found other doors into the written record. In the K-drama Rookie Historian Goo Hae-ryung, a woman walks into the palace as an official historian — a thrilling premise and a historical invention.
era: Joseon Dynasty (1392–1910)

title: Why Prince Sado Died in a Rice Chest: Joseon's Most Shocking Royal Tragedy
description: In the film The Throne (사도, 2015), King Yeongjo locks Crown Prince Sado inside a wooden rice chest for eight days. Here's the real history — the Imo Incident of 1762, the factional war between Noron and Soron, and why a king chose a legal gray zone over a formal execution — compared with Peter the Great, Suleiman the Magnificent, and Shakespeare.
era: Late Joseon Dynasty (18th century)

title: Warrior K (무신), Explained: Why an Army Kept Fighting After the King Surrendered
description: MBC's 2012 epic Musin (Warrior K) follows Kim Jun through Goryeo's military-regime era — but the real climax comes after the drama's final episode. When the Goryeo court submitted to the Mongols in 1270, one elite unit, the Sambyeolcho, refused to go home and fought on for three more years, from Jindo to Jeju. Here's the true story, and how it echoes the Southern Song's own doomed holdout against the same empire.
era: Goryeo (13th century)

title: Did the Sambyeolcho Escape to Okinawa? The Mystery of a Goryeo-Inscribed Roof Tile
description: The Sambyeolcho story usually ends in 1273 on Jeju Island, crushed by a Mongol-Goryeo army. But a roof tile in Okinawa — stamped 'made by a Goryeo tile-maker' — has led some scholars to ask whether part of the rebellion escaped across the sea. Here's the real archaeology behind the mystery, and why it's a fascinating hypothesis, not a settled fact.
era: Goryeo Dynasty (918–1392)

show: The Dream Life of Mr. Kim
title: When Did Koreans Start Grilling Samgyeopsal? The History Behind The Dream Life of Mr. Kim
description: In JTBC's The Dream Life of Mr. Kim, a department head whose company dinner falls through ends up grilling pork belly alone. Nobody knows exactly when Koreans began grilling samgyeopsal: the cut is named in Korean print in the 1930s, while restaurants specialising in grilling it become visible only in the late 1970s. This article dates the famous origin stories — the coal miners, the exports to Japan, the portable gas burner — against that gap, and finds that each of them fails in a different way.
drama: The Dream Life of Mr. Kim (서울 자가에 대기업 다니는 김 부장 이야기, JTBC, 2025) — a 12-part Saturday–Sunday drama that ran from 25 October to 30 November 2025, directed by Cho Hyun-tak and adapted from Song Hee-gu's novel, with Ryu Seung-ryong as Kim Nak-soo: a department head at a large company who owns his own apartment in Seoul and is about to lose the identity assembled from both. Note for readers of our earlier piece: Koreans shorten this title to 'Kim Bujang', which is also the Korean short form of the unrelated SBS series Agent Kim Reactivated. Two different dramas, one nickname.
era: Modern and contemporary Korea — the cut is named in 1930s print, the grilling culture is visible from the late 1970s, the word standardises in the 1980s, and the origin legends surface later still
tags: The Dream Life of Mr. Kim

show: Dae Jang Geum / Jewel in the Palace
title: Seokbinggo, Explained: How Joseon Stored Winter Ice — and Who the Law Let Have It
description: Joseon cut ice from the frozen Han in midwinter and kept it until summer in state ice houses. Who received it was written into the law code — and the list runs from royal kin and senior officials to the sick and to prisoners in jail.
drama: Dae Jang Geum / Jewel in the Palace (대장금, MBC, 2003–2004) · Bon Appétit, Your Majesty (폭군의 셰프, Netflix, 2025)
era: Joseon — the Gyeongguk daejeon ice regulations; surviving stone ice houses of the 18th century

title: How Korea's Seokbinggo Compares with Persia's Yakhchāl and Japan's Himuro
description: Three societies solved the same problem before refrigeration: keeping ice until summer. The engineering differences matter less than a question each answered differently — who the ice was for, and where that rule was written down.
drama: Companion piece to the Joseon ice-house post — anchored on Dae Jang Geum (대장금) and Bon Appétit, Your Majesty (폭군의 셰프)
era: Sasanian and Islamic Iran · Heian Japan · Joseon Korea

title: Why a Silla Royal Tomb Is Guarded by a Face That Looks West Asian
description: In front of the Gyeongju tomb identified as that of King Wonseong of Unified Silla (r. 785–798) stands a stone military figure with deep-set eyes, a high nose and a curled beard — features that have long been read as Central or West Asian. This article asks what that sculpture does and does not prove, working from the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture, Urihistorynet, the National Gugak Center and published scholarship, and it keeps the distinction the sources keep: between an actual West Asian person and an international guardian image that Silla received and reworked. Hwarang (화랑, KBS2, 2016–2017) is set some two hundred years earlier and never touches the subject; it is used here as a contrast, not as evidence.
drama: Hwarang: The Poet Warrior Youth (화랑, KBS2, 19 December 2016 – 21 February 2017, 20 episodes). Overseas availability on Netflix, Rakuten Viki and Kocowa varies by country and by date, and should be re-checked in the reader's own territory
era: Unified Silla — the Gyeongju tomb identified as King Wonseong's (r. 785–798) and its stone figures; with fifth- to sixth-century Silla tombs, the reign of King Heongang (r. 875–886), and the mid-sixth-century reign of King Jinheung that the drama depicts, all held apart rather than merged

title: Why Do Korean Parents Hire Admissions Coordinators? SKY Castle & Korea's 600-Year Exam Obsession, Explained
description: In SKY Castle, elite parents hire a private 'admissions coordinator' to engineer their child's path into Korea's top universities. Here's the real history behind Korea's exam obsession — from the Joseon civil-service exam to the ₩27.5-trillion private-tutoring market — and how it compares with China, India, and the US.
era: Contemporary South Korea (with Joseon-era roots)

title: Road to Boston, Explained: They Erased the Flag from the Photograph. Ninety Years Later, the Official Result Still Says Japan.
description: The 2023 film Road to Boston opens on a podium in Berlin, 1936, where a Korean marathon champion stands while the Japanese anthem plays. Two Korean newspapers then did something almost unheard of in press history: they retouched the flag off his chest in the photograph. One paper was suspended for 278 days and eight staff were jailed; the other never came back.
