This article checks the story against the records — and finds that the film's slogan, 'if the country became independent, our records should be independent too,' is still not true. In the IOC's official results the 1936 marathon champion is registered as Kitei Son of Japan — even though the IOC's own biography has identified him as Korean since 2011. The article also corrects three things the popular telling gets wrong about his times, including the claim that he was the first human under 2:30.
drama: Road to Boston (1947 보스톤, 2023, dir. Kang Je-gyu, 108 min) — Ha Jung-woo as Sohn Kee-chung, Im Si-wan as Suh Yun-bok; on the first Korean team to run the Boston Marathon under its own flag
era: Japanese colonial period — the 1936 Berlin Olympics and the flag erasure incident of August 1936; the record dispute continues to 2026

title: Squid Game's Dalgona Candy, Explained: The Real Korean Childhood Game Turned Deadly
description: In Squid Game, the dalgona challenge turns a beloved Korean street candy into a death game. Here's the real history behind dalgona — why it's soaked in nostalgia, what the ppopgi game actually rewarded, and how a poor generation's cheap sweet became the show's most quietly devastating prop.
era: Contemporary South Korea / 20th-century nostalgia

title: Squid Game, Explained: Why Would Anyone Risk Their Life in a Game Over Debt?
description: In Squid Game, hundreds of people vote to leave a deadly contest — and then most of them come back. Here's what South Korean household debt actually measures, what the 1997 crisis actually did to Korean working life, and why Gi-hun's layoff has a documented real-world source.
era: Contemporary South Korea

title: Netflix's Mr. Queen, Explained: Why Did Joseon's Queen Dowagers Rule From Behind a Screen?
description: In Mr. Queen, an old dowager's quiet word can outweigh a minister's. That's not sageuk flavor — it's suryeom cheongjeong, Joseon's official mechanism for a royal woman to sit in on government from behind a screen, and Queen Dowager Sunwon is the only woman in Joseon history who did it twice.
era: Joseon dynasty (1392–1897)

show: The King of Tears, Lee Bang-won
title: KBS's The King of Tears, Lee Bang-won, Explained: Why Yi Bang-won Killed Two Half-Brothers — but Spared the Brother Who Attacked Him
description: In KBS's The King of Tears, Lee Bang-won, a founding prince turns on his own family to seize the throne. Here's the real Strife of Princes behind the drama — and how Joseon, the Ottomans, the Mughals and Europe each faced the same danger differently: what stops a king's sons from fighting over the throne?
drama: The King of Tears, Lee Bang-won (태종 이방원, 2021–2022, KBS1)
era: Joseon Dynasty — founding generation, 1392–1418 (Taejo to Taejong)

title: Take Charge of My Heart, Explained: Korea's Chaebol Feuds and the 'Strife of Princes'
description: In Netflix's Take Charge of My Heart (2026), the heir's rivals are relatives. Five selected, widely reported control fights (Hyundai 2000 and 2003, Doosan 2005, Lotte 2015, Hanjin 2020) also pitted relatives against each other, and the press called them the 'Strife of Princes.' Here's what those cases show and where they were decided.
drama: Take Charge of My Heart (나를 충전해줘, Netflix, 2026)
era: Modern South Korea (chaebol succession disputes, 2000–2020)

title: Netflix's Teach You a Lesson, Explained: Where Did the Korean Teacher's Rod Get Its Authority?
description: Teachers' and parents' groups held a press conference outside Netflix Korea against Teach You a Lesson (참교육) before it was released. Both sides of the argument assume a teacher's authority is something the state grants. Joseon ran two systems at once: village schools that depended on the families who supported them, and state schools governed by a written code. Here is what the records actually show.
era: Joseon Dynasty (1392–1910) to the present

title: Why Revenge Feels Like Justice in The Glory: Korea's School Violence Crisis, Explained
description: In The Glory, Moon Dong-eun spends sixteen years dismantling her abusers without ever relying on the police. Here's the real history behind that choice — Korea's School Violence Prevention Act, the face culture that complicates reporting, the school record that can shape a college future, and how Korea's approach compares with Japan's ijime system, America's zero-tolerance era, and European restorative justice.
era: Contemporary South Korea (with historical roots in social hierarchy and face culture)

title: The Great Battle, Explained: Was Yeon Gaesomun a Villain or a Defender of Goguryeo?
description: In The Great Battle (안시성, 2018), Goguryeo's strongman Yeon Gaesomun sends an assassin after the commander of Ansi Fortress. Such an order does not appear in the major surviving accounts consulted for this article. What they do have is a single line from the Tang emperor, who is recorded as saying he had heard that this same fortress had once refused to submit to Yeon Gaesomun and that Yeon had failed to take it. Here is the man behind the film's villain: he killed a king, and Goguryeo was not conquered by Tang during his lifetime; it fell in 668, after his death and amid a succession struggle among his sons. Korea's oldest surviving history placed his biography beside a king-deposer's; an exiled Korean writer of the early twentieth century made him a hero; the Chinese opera stage made him a knife-throwing enemy general.
drama: The Great Battle (안시성, 2018, feature film, dir. Kim Kwang-sik)
era: Goguryeo, 642–668 CE: Yeon Gaesomun's coup, the Goguryeo–Tang War of 645, and the fall of Goguryeo

title: The Scandal, Explained: Why a Joseon Household Took In a Concubine for an Heir — and Why Her Son Might Never Become One
description: In Netflix's The Scandal, a Joseon minister's household takes in a young concubine to get an heir, and his wife's scheming turns on the child she might bear. Here's what Joseon law actually said about wives, concubines, and their sons: who could carry on the family rites (as distinct from who received property), why upper-class households often turned to adoption within the patriline instead, how concubines' sons were barred first from the exams and then from the elite posts, and how Song China, the Ottoman court, and Meiji Japan handled the same question differently.
era: Joseon Dynasty — King Jeongjo's era (late 18th century), Bukchon, Hanyang

title: Jeong Do-jeon, Explained: Why Ming China Wouldn't Recognize Korea's New King for Nine Years
description: In the 2014 KBS drama Jeong Do-jeon, a dispute over the wording of a diplomatic document spirals into executions and a planned invasion of Ming territory. Here's the real, unresolved crisis behind it — and why, for nine years, the founder of a brand-new dynasty ruled at home while China still refused to officially recognize him as king.
era: Late Goryeo–early Joseon transition, 1392–1403

title: Bon Appétit, Your Majesty Explained: Joseon Royal Food Tasters, Gimi Sanggung, and the King's Table
description: Someone tasted the Joseon king's food before he did — but the gimi sanggung everyone pictures belongs to one late tradition, and in 1765 the job fell to pharmacy officials and a eunuch. What the tyrant's chef drama sharpens, and what the record actually shows about the surasang, the palace kitchens and gamseon.
drama: Bon Appétit, Your Majesty (폭군의 셰프, tvN, 2025)
era: Joseon — Yeonsangun's reign (1494–1506); court food traditions transmitted from the Gojong and Sunjong era

title: Nine Daughters, One Outside Son-in-Law — and He Had Already Surrendered His Kingdom
description: Goryeo's founder Wang Geon took twenty-nine consorts from powerful houses across the peninsula. He had nine daughters. Of the eight whose marriages the record names, six were inside the royal family, including to half-brothers. The two who married out married the same man — Kim Bu, the last king of Silla, and only after he had come over and given up his kingdom.
drama: Moon Lovers: Scarlet Heart Ryeo (달의 연인 — 보보경심 려, SBS, 2016)
era: Early Goryeo — the reign of Taejo Wang Geon (918–943) and the succession that followed

title: Warrior K (무신), Explained: Why Did Goryeo Move Its Capital to an Island — and Who Made the Decision?
description: In MBC's Warrior K, King Gojong leaves Gaegyeong at Choe U's urging. The chronicles tell a darker story: the decisive council on the 1232 move to Ganghwa Island was convened at Choe U's own house, the king is recorded as hesitating, and an officer who argued for defending the old capital was beheaded. Here is why the island was chosen, who decided, and what the mainland paid from 1232 until the return to Gaegyeong in 1270.
era: Goryeo, 1231–1270 (the Mongol invasions and the 1232 move of the capital to Ganghwa Island)

title: My Dearest and Joseon's Jungin Interpreters: Rich, Powerful, but Never Yangban
description: MBC's My Dearest gives its male lead a family line of professional interpreters. That detail opens onto one of Joseon Korea's strangest social puzzles: the jungin class — technical experts who could out-earn noblemen and still never become one. Here's the real history of yeokgwan interpreters, the japgwa exam, and the Bureau of Interpreters.
era: Joseon dynasty — jungin class structure

title: Knight Flower, Explained: Why a Chaste Widow Became One of Joseon's Highest Public Honors
description: In MBC's Knight Flower, a noblewoman lives two lives — a model chaste widow by day, a masked vigilante by night. Here's the real history behind the daytime role: Joseon Korea's widow remarriage ban, the yeollyeo-mun chastity-gate honor system, and how a woman's only path to public honor could also become a trap.
era: Joseon dynasty (1392–1910), chastity ideology intensifying from the 17th century onward

title: Bloody Heart, Explained: Yeonjwaje, the Joseon Law That Could Destroy a Traitor's Whole Family
description: In KBS2's Bloody Heart, one household's downfall becomes an entire family's execution. Here's the real Joseon-era law behind it — yeonjwaje, the Ming legal code Korea adopted, the doctrine of 'three kindred' liability, and how the U.S. Constitution wrote the exact opposite rule into its own founding text.
era: Joseon

title: Bloody Heart, Explained: Did Ancient Rome Have a Version of Joseon's Yeonjwaje?
description: In Bloody Heart (붉은 단심), a treason charge doesn't end with one person — it can destroy an entire family. That's Joseon's yeonjwaje, guilt by association. But was punishing a traitor's family a uniquely 'Eastern' idea? Ancient Rome had its own version. Here's how Joseon and Rome both made treason a family catastrophe — and why the way they did it was strikingly different.
era: Joseon Dynasty (1392–1910)

title: Reply 1988, Explained: How Yeontan Shaped Winter Life in a 1980s Seoul Alley
description: The neighbors in Reply 1988 (응답하라 1988) are always in each other's homes because of living conditions, not just sentiment: close-set houses, shared outdoor space, and yeontan (coal briquette) heating gave them practical reasons to help one another. Yeontan consumption rose from 20.83 million tons in 1980 to 26.92 million tons in 1986, so in 1988 it was still near the center of urban winter life. The briquette, and the carbon-monoxide danger that came with it, helped build the warmth of a Korean alley.
era: Modern Korea (1988)
